# What this tutorial is

`docs/multiphysics.md` presents the multiphysics examples as results. This tutorial is the same
material as a procedure. Each section explains the physics, then gives the commands that produce
each figure, then explains every flag, analysis card and model parameter those commands depend
on. It also says why each one is there: what goes wrong, or what the run would cost, without it.

The examples, in the order they were built:

| § | Example | Domains | What it exercises in the simulator |
|---|---|---|---|
| [3](#peltier) | Peltier cooler under PID control | electrical, thermal (absolute K) | `.dc` sweep, `.op`, transient with a controller, `@(timer)`, `laplace_nd`, `transition` |
| [4](#mems) | Electrostatic MEMS actuator | electrical, mechanical, thermal | `.dc` continuation through pull-in, `.ac` small-signal, `PWL` transient with contact events |
| [5](#reram) | Filamentary ReRAM | electrical, thermal, filament gap | stiff switching, `$bound_step`, `analysis("static")`, step size scaled with frequency |
| [6](#axon) | Hodgkin–Huxley axon | electrical, gating, chemistry | `generate` loops, vector nets, structural parameter overrides, sparse solve |
| [7](#grid) | Power-grid swing | electromechanical | nonlinear load flow as a DC point, relays as events, cascades |
| [8](#ring) | Thermo-optic ring bank | optical, thermal, control | a stiff ps/ms system, complex ODEs as node pairs, PI locks, bistability |
| [9](#liion) | Li-ion cell | electrochemical, thermal | diffusion ladders, inverted Butler–Volmer, aging over years, runaway in seconds |
| [10](#relay) | Electromagnetic relay | electrical, magnetic, mechanical, thermal | Jiles–Atherton hysteresis, contact bounce, hot pickup, remanence |
| [11](#grayscott) | Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion | chemical kinetics on a grid | a PDE as a 2-D vector net, event `or` lists, file output from a model |

Every number quoted below was measured with the command shown next to it. Each figure is the
file in `docs/examples/multiphysics/` that the command writes.

::: {.callout-note}
These examples are checked against closed-form results and conservation laws, which each section
states. Unlike the decks under `golden/`, they are **not** validated against a reference
simulator: QSPICE cannot run these models.
:::

# Getting set up, and how a run is put together

## Build, and a name for the binary

From the repository root:

```bash
cargo build --release
```

The binary is `target/release/va-cli` (`va-cli.exe` on Windows). The commands below call it
`va-cli`, as the deck headers do. Make that name work in your shell:

```bash
# bash / Git Bash / zsh
alias va-cli="$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

```powershell
# PowerShell
Set-Alias va-cli "$PWD\target\release\va-cli.exe"
```

The figures that need more than one plot of raw quantities are drawn by small Python scripts in
`docs/examples/multiphysics/`, which need Python 3 and `matplotlib`. Each script runs the
simulator itself and takes the binary's path as an argument:

```bash
python docs/examples/multiphysics/reram_iv.py "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Windows: give the scripts an absolute path

Python's `subprocess` on Windows does not resolve a relative, forward-slash path such as
`target/release/va-cli`, and fails with `FileNotFoundError`. Pass the absolute path:
`"$(pwd -W)/target/release/va-cli.exe"` in Git Bash, or
`"$PWD\target\release\va-cli.exe"` in PowerShell.
:::

## The three inputs of a run

```bash
va-cli sim <deck.net> --model <library directory> [--tran | --ac | --noise] [--report a,b,...] [--plot out.svg]
```

**The model library** (`--model models/multiphysics/tec`). A *directory* is compiled as one
unit: every `.va` and `.vams` file in it is parsed, then every module is elaborated against all
of them. Each example therefore keeps its modules and its `nature`/`discipline` declarations
(`tec_natures.vams`, `mems_natures.vams`, …) together in one directory. Each `.va` file pulls the
declarations in with `` `include ``, which resolves against the file's own directory. A deck that
needs two libraries can repeat `--model`.

**The deck** (`circuits/multiphysics/*.net`) is a SPICE-like netlist:

```text
* comment lines start with a star; the first lines of every deck explain it
V1 drv gnd DC 0                      voltage source: DC, AC, SIN(...), PWL(...), PULSE(...)
G1 gnd stim p gnd 1e-6               voltage-controlled current source (out+ out- ctl+ ctl- gain)
R1 in te 2k                          resistor
X1 drv gnd cold hot tec alpha1=0     a Verilog-A module: ports, module name, parameter overrides
.tran 0.5 150                        the analysis card
.end
```

An `X` line places a Verilog-A module. Its terminals come first, in the order of the module's
port list, then the module name, then any `name=value` overrides of its parameters. Every
example uses overrides to configure one model several ways: `pressure=1` vs `pressure=100`,
`tamb=300` vs `tamb=400`, `tc=18.5` vs `tc=6.3`.

**The analysis**: a card in the deck, plus a flag that must agree with it.

| Deck card | Flag | Analysis |
|---|---|---|
| `.op` | none | DC operating point |
| `.dc V1 0 20 0.25` | none | DC sweep of a source |
| `.ac lin 4001 8410 10410` | `--ac` | small-signal AC around the operating point |
| `.tran 0.5 150` | `--tran` | transient |
| `.noise …` | `--noise` | noise |

A deck with a `.tran` card run without `--tran` is refused, rather than quietly run as DC:

```text
Error: deck requests transient analysis (`.tran`); pass `--tran` to run it
```

## Naming what you want to see: `--report`

Without `--report`, every unknown is printed. With it, only the named quantities are printed and
plotted. A name can be:

- a net of the deck: `cold`, `x`, `g1`;
- a device's current: `V1` (a voltage source's branch current);
- a node *inside* an instance, by hierarchical name: `X1.g` (the ReRAM's gap node),
  `XA1.w` (a machine's speed node), `X1.v[50]` (element 50 of a vector net),
  `X1.dnai[5]` (the thin fibre's sodium in compartment 5).

Each value is printed with the **access function of its nature**, not as a voltage. A thermal
node prints `Temp(cold) = 277.705459 K`, a mechanical node `Pos(x) = 4.574131e-8 m`, the ReRAM
gap `Gap(X1.g)`, a machine's speed `Om(XA1.w)`. Those names come from the `nature` declarations
in each library's `.vams` file (`access = Temp;`, `units = "K";`). Declaring natures this way is
how a model says what its unknowns *are*. It is also what makes each unknown's convergence
tolerance its own (the nature's `abstol`), rather than one tolerance in volts for everything.

## Plots: `--plot`, or a script

`--plot out.svg` writes one SVG of every reported quantity, against time (transient), against the
swept source (`.dc`), or as a Bode plot (`.ac`). That is enough for most of the figures here. A
Python script is used where the figure needs a quantity the simulator does not report
(a current computed from two node voltages, a Nernst potential, a frequency in Hz), several runs
on one axis, or data the model wrote to a file.

## How a transient run is controlled

`.tran <tstep> <tstop> [UIC]` means something specific here:

- **`tstep` is the maximum time step**, not an output grid. The step controller starts at
  `tstep` and only ever shrinks below it, to keep the local truncation error within
  `reltol·|x| + abstol` (defaults `1e-3` and the nature's own `abstol`). It also lands exactly on
  every breakpoint: a `PWL`/`PULSE` corner, an `@(timer)` instant, a `cross` event bracketed in
  time. The pre-flight line counts the resulting floor:
  `~301 points (adaptive, 301 is the card's floor)` for `.tran 0.5 150`.
  The run usually takes more points than that floor, wherever something fast happens.
- **Choosing `tstep` is a modelling decision**, and every example below says why its value was
  chosen. Too large, and a slow-looking stretch hides an event, or the step is long enough to
  change an answer that converges with the step. Too small, and the run costs more than the
  physics needs. The examples check their important numbers at two caps (§5, §6, §7).
- **The run starts from the DC operating point** unless the card says `UIC`. None of these decks
  uses `UIC`. With it, every unknown would start at zero, and zero is not a harmless start for a
  physical model: for the Peltier cooler it is 0 K. Where a *state* needs a chosen starting value
  rather than its equilibrium (the ReRAM gap, the concentrations of the axon), the model pins it
  in the operating point with `analysis("static")`. Each example shows how.
- Integration is trapezoidal (second order) by default; `--integration be|trap|gear` changes it.
  None of the examples needs to.

Before solving, `sim` prints what it is about to do, for example:

```text
[va-cli] circuit: 7 device(s) (7 compiled), 10 unknown(s) (4 net(s) + 6 auxiliary row(s)), ~301 points (adaptive, 301 is the card's floor)
[va-cli] estimate: 14-635 ms of solve, 2.4 kB of matrix — rough, dense LU scaled from bench-scale on an i7-1185G7
[va-cli] linear solve: dense LU (10 < 100 unknowns)
```

*Auxiliary rows* are unknowns the models create inside themselves (internal nodes, state
variables). The linear solver is chosen by size: dense below 100 unknowns, sparse from 100
(`--solver auto`, the default). The axon (903 unknowns) runs sparse; everything else runs dense.

## What the models print

Every model here reports its own events with `$strobe`. These lines arrive on standard output,
interleaved with the results and prefixed with the instance name (`%m`):

```text
XP: loop closed at t=5 s
XP: within 0.1 K of the setpoint at t=30.86 s (drive 4.222 V)
XL: heat load steps from 1 W to 3 W at t=60 s
```

Many of the checks below are read straight off these lines.

## Options these examples do *not* use, and why

| Option | What it does | Why it is not used here |
|---|---|---|
| `--bypass` | reuses a device's last evaluation while its terminals barely move | results are not bit-identical; it pays off on large transistor circuits, not on a handful of models |
| `--reltol`, `--abstol`, `--newton-reltol` | loosen step and Newton tolerances | defaults are what every quoted number was measured with |
| `--threads <n>` | evaluates instances in parallel | results are identical at every count; these circuits have one to twenty instances |
| `--tasks-once` | prints each distinct `$strobe` line once | the examples' strobes are events that should all be seen |
| `--solver dense\|sparse` | overrides the size rule | the automatic choice is right for every example |

# Peltier cooler under PID control {#peltier}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/tec/`, which contains:

- `tec.va`: the thermoelectric module;
- `thermal_parts.va`: `thermal_mass`, `thermal_res`, `ambient`, `heat_load`;
- `pid.va`: the controller;
- `tec_natures.vams`: the `thermal_abs` discipline, with temperature in **kelvin above 0 K** and heat in watts.

**Why absolute temperature.** The Peltier heat at a junction is α·I·T, with T the junction's
*absolute* temperature. A "temperature rise above ambient" discipline would make every Peltier
term wrong by α·I·T_ambient. The `ambient` module is therefore a temperature source of
298.15 K. It is also the first reason these decks never use `UIC`: a zero start would be 0 K.

The module's Seebeck coefficient depends on temperature, α(T) = α₀ + α₁(T − 300 K), with
resistance R(T) = R₀(1 + tcr·(T − 300 K)). The Peltier, Joule and conduction heats follow from
that, and so does the Thomson heat, which is what makes the energy balance close.

## Maximum temperature difference (DC sweep)

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/tec_dtmax.net --model models/multiphysics/tec --report cold --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/tec_dtmax.svg
```

![The cold face's temperature against drive voltage](examples/multiphysics/tec_dtmax.svg)

**The deck.** The drive is swept 0 → 20 V by `.dc V1 0 20 0.25`. The hot face is held at 300 K
by `XA hot ambient tamb=300` and the cold face is insulated: the module is the only thing
touching it.

**The parameters that matter.** `alpha1=0 tcr=0` on the module's line switch off the
temperature dependence of α and R. That is not a simplification for its own sake: it is what
makes the textbook closed form apply. With α and R constant, the cold face is coldest where the
extra heat pumped by more current equals the extra Joule heat it brings, I = α·T_c/R, which
gives **T_c = 232.455 K (ΔT = 67.545 K) at 5.811 A, 15.00 V**.

**Check.** The sweep's minimum is 232.4555 K at 15.00 V and 5.8114 A. Past it the cold face warms
again. Add `V1` to `--report` to see the current alongside.

## Energy audit (operating point)

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/tec_energy.net --model models/multiphysics/tec
```

No plot: this is a single `.op`, and the check is arithmetic on what it prints.

```text
DC operating point:
  V(drv) = 5.000000 V
  Temp(cold) = 277.705459 K
  Temp(hot) = 303.144232 K
  Temp(amb) = 298.150000 K
  I(V1) = -1.950932e0 A
  XA.b0 = 9.754658e0
```

The full module (α₁ = 10⁻⁴ V/K², tcr = 0.4 %/K) at 5 V, with each face tied to a 298.15 K
ambient through a thermal resistance: 2 K/W on the cold side, 0.25 K/W on the hot side.

| Quantity | How it is read off the output | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Q_c, heat pumped | (298.15 − Temp(cold)) / 2 | 10.2223 W |
| Q_h, heat rejected | (Temp(hot) − 298.15) / 0.25 | 19.9769 W |
| P_e, electrical power | 5 × (−I(V1)) | 9.7547 W |

**Q_h − Q_c − P_e = −2.5·10⁻⁶ W**, which is the print precision (temperatures to 10⁻⁶ K,
divided by 0.25 K/W).

The last line, `XA.b0`, is the ambient source's own branch flow: the net heat the ambient
absorbs, 9.754658 W. It is P_e, as conservation requires at steady state: everything the
electrical side puts in ends up in the ambient. Delete the Thomson term from `tec.va` and the
balance is off by I·α₁·(T_h² − T_c²)/2 = 1.44 W.

## Closed-loop regulation through a load step (transient)

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/tec_pid.net --model models/multiphysics/tec --tran --report plate,sink --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/tec_pid_temps.svg
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/tec_pid.net --model models/multiphysics/tec --tran --report drv --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/tec_pid_drive.svg
```

The same run twice, reporting different quantities, because temperatures (~300 K) and the drive
(0–12 V) would share one axis badly.

![Plate and heat-sink temperatures](examples/multiphysics/tec_pid_temps.svg)
![The controller's drive voltage](examples/multiphysics/tec_pid_drive.svg)

**The deck.**

- **The plant.** A 20 J/K plate (`XM1 … thermal_mass C=20`) carries a heat load of 1 W
  (`XL … heat_load p0=1 dp=2 tstep=60 trise=0.5`), stepping by +2 W at 60 s. The module's hot
  face sits on a 50 J/K sink, 0.5 K/W to the ambient.
- **The controller.** `XP plate drv pid tset=278.15 kp=2 ki=0.2 kd=2 tf=0.5 kb=1 vmin=0 vmax=12 ton=5`
  reads the plate's temperature and drives the module.

**What each controller parameter is for.**

- `kp`, `ki`, `kd` are the PID gains, in V/K, V/(K·s) and V·s/K.
- `tf=0.5` filters the derivative, (s/(1 + s·tf)), so the D term does not amplify the
  step-to-step noise of the solution. It is implemented as `laplace_nd` on an internal node of its own.
  The Laplace operators are only accepted as a *whole* contribution to a node, not inside a
  larger expression. Giving the filter its own node is how a model uses one as a building block.
- `vmin=0 vmax=12` are the supply's rails. `kb=1` is the back-calculation anti-windup: while the
  output is clamped at a rail, the integrator is bled toward the clamped value. With `kb=0` the
  integrator winds up during the 12 V saturation at start-up, and the plate undershoots to
  272.94 K, 5.2 K below the setpoint. With `kb=1` its lowest point is 278.00 K, within the
  0.1 K band.
- `ton=5` closes the loop at 5 s, through `@(timer(ton))`. Before that, and in the operating point
  the run starts from, the drive is 0. The run therefore starts from the *uncooled* steady state
  (plate 299.79 K) instead of from an artificial zero.
- The loop is switched in through `transition(en, 0, 0.2)`, a 0.2 s ramp. Switched in as a bare
  step, the drive would jump by several volts within one time step, and the step controller would
  shrink the step until it underflowed: no step is short enough to make a discontinuity smooth.

**The `.tran 0.5 150` card.** The plate's time constant is tens of seconds (20 J/K against the
module's conductance), so a 0.5 s cap still resolves every transient, and the controller's
fastest dynamics (the 0.2 s ramp, the 0.5 s derivative filter) are resolved by the step
controller shrinking below the cap. The run takes 553 points.

**What the strobes say, and the figure shows.**

```text
XP: loop closed at t=5 s
XP: within 0.1 K of the setpoint at t=30.86 s (drive 4.222 V)
XL: heat load steps from 1 W to 3 W at t=60 s
```

1. The loop closes at 5 s and the drive sits at the 12 V rail for about a second. The plate
   falls 21.6 K and enters the 0.1 K band at **t = 30.86 s** without undershooting.
2. The sink warms to 311.7 K, carrying the pumped heat plus all the electrical power, then
   relaxes as the drive falls to about 3.4 V.
3. At 60 s the load steps to 3 W. The plate rises by 0.18 K, the drive answers, and the plate is
   back at 278.147 K at 150 s.

# Electrostatic MEMS: pull-in, damping, contact and stiction {#mems}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/mems/mems_parts.va`, with composable parts on one mechanical
node:

- `proof_mass`;
- `spring`;
- `es_gap`, the parallel-plate transducer;
- `squeeze_film`, gas damping with rarefaction;
- `thermoelastic`;
- `contact`, Hertzian landing plus adhesion.

`mems_natures.vams` defines `MEMS_EPS0` and the mechanical disciplines.

**Position as a potential.** The mechanical node's potential is the plate's displacement and its
flow is force, so Kirchhoff's current law at the node *is* Newton's second law: spring, damping,
electrostatic and contact forces summing to m·ẍ. Each effect is a separate module on the same
node (`XK x spring`, `XM x proof_mass`, `XS x squeeze_film`, …). A deck composes the device, and
removing a line removes an effect.

The device: a 100 µm square plate, 2 µm above an electrode covered by 0.1 µm of dielectric
(εᵣ = 7.5), on a 1 N/m spring, which resonates near 10 kHz.

## Pull-in (DC sweep)

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/mems_pullin.net --model models/multiphysics/mems --report x --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/mems_pullin.svg
```

![Static deflection against voltage, through pull-in](examples/multiphysics/mems_pullin.svg)

**Why a sweep, and why its step matters.** A `.dc` sweep starts each point's Newton solve from the
previous point's solution. That is what lets it follow the *stable* branch of a system with
several equilibria. Below pull-in the plate has two equilibria, stable and unstable. The sweep
stays on the stable one because it starts there, with `.dc V1 0 8 0.05` in 0.05 V steps, each a
small continuation step. At pull-in that branch ends, and the next point can only land on the
contact branch, at the dielectric stop at x = 1.9 µm.

**Closed form.** The effective gap is g₀ + t_d/εᵣ = 2.01333 µm.
V_PI = √(8k·g_e³/(27ε₀A)) = **5.2259 V**, at x = g_e/3 = 0.67111 µm. Below pull-in the deck's
header lists checkpoints from k·x = ε₀AV²/(2(g_e − x)²), and the sweep reproduces them:
x = 4.574131·10⁻⁸ m at 2 V and 4.568402·10⁻⁷ m at 5 V (closed form 0.04574 µm and 0.45684 µm).

## Resonance under bias, at two pressures (AC)

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/mems_resonance.net --model models/multiphysics/mems --ac --report xlo,xhi --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/mems_resonance.svg
```

![Small-signal response at 1 Pa and 100 Pa](examples/multiphysics/mems_resonance.svg)

**The deck.** Two copies of the device in one netlist: `xlo` in a 1 Pa package and `xhi` at
100 Pa (`squeeze_film pressure=1` vs `pressure=100`). Both are driven by `V1 drv gnd DC 3 AC 1`:
the `DC 3` sets the bias the AC analysis linearises about, and `AC 1` is the small-signal
amplitude.

**The `.ac lin 4001 8410 10410` card** puts 4001 points linearly between 8.41 and 10.41 kHz, a
0.5 Hz grid around the resonance. The grid matters for the Q measurement. At 1 Pa the
half-power width is only 5.9 Hz, so a coarse grid misplaces the peak and the half-power points.
On this grid the measured Q is 1603.6; on a 2.5 mHz grid around the peak it is 1605.2, which is
the model's own value.

**What the physics predicts.**

- **Frequency.** The 3 V bias softens the spring by ε₀AV²/g³ = 0.1156 N/m, and the
  thermoelastic coupling stiffens it by 4.7·10⁻⁴ N/m. The resonance moves from 10006 Hz to
  **9412.55 Hz** in both packages.
- **Damping at 1 Pa.** The rarefied gas barely damps, and thermoelastic loss limits
  **Q to 1605**.
- **Damping at 100 Pa.** The squeeze film dominates: **Q = 78.2**.

The thermoelastic damping is not a fitted Q. The `thermoelastic` module couples the plate to a
thermal mode with τ = 15.9 µs, and Zener's frequency-dependent loss comes out of the circuit.

## Pull-in, bounce, stiction and release (transient)

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/mems_hysteresis.net --model models/multiphysics/mems --tran --report x --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/mems_hysteresis.svg
```

![Displacement through a slow voltage triangle](examples/multiphysics/mems_hysteresis.svg)

**The deck.** `V1 drv gnd PWL(0 0 5m 7 10m 0)` is a 0 → 7 → 0 V triangle over 10 ms, at 100 Pa.
Each corner of a `PWL` source is a breakpoint the step controller lands on.

**The `.tran 2u 10m` card.** The plate's period is 0.1 ms, so a 2 µs cap gives at least 50 steps
per oscillation, and the controller shrinks further during each impact. Every bounce on the
Hertzian contact lasts microseconds, and the `contact` model counts them (`tbounce=50e-6`: a
contact shorter than 50 µs is a bounce). A cap of the order of the period would skip most of
them. The run takes 13,075 points in about 1.4 s.

**What the contact model reports.**

```text
XC: landed   at t=3.8424e-03 s, V=5.3794 V
XC: released at t=9.4973e-03 s, V=0.7038 V (the landing bounced 48 times)
```

- **Landing.** The plate lands at 5.38 V. That is V_PI plus the time the snap takes: about one
  period (0.11 ms) to travel 1.3 µm.
- **Release.** It releases at **0.7038 V**, against the closed form
  √(2g_c²(k·x_c − f_a)/(ε₀A)) = 0.7023 V. In contact the gap is only the 0.1 µm dielectric, so
  the same voltage pulls about 316 times harder.
- **Adhesion.** The 0.2 µN adhesion (`fa=2e-7`) moves release from 0.742 V down to 0.702 V.
  That is stiction, the reason RF-MEMS switches fail to release.

**A modelling note.** The Hertzian force is written as an explicit branch,
`if (d > 0.0) fc = kc*d*sqrt(d); else fc = 0.0;`, rather than `pow(max(d, 0), 1.5)`. Differentiating the latter at
d ≤ 0 gives 0·∞ = NaN in the Jacobian, and d < 0 is every point before contact. The adhesion is
switched on smoothly by a logistic in d, written in a form whose `exp` never overflows. Whatever
a Newton solver differentiates must stay finite wherever it is evaluated, including at the
corner of a `max`.

# Filamentary ReRAM: filament growth, Joule heating, Arrhenius drift {#reram}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/reram/`: `reram.va` and `reram_natures.vams`, which defines a
`gap_disc` discipline whose potential is the filament gap in nanometres.

The cell's state is the gap g between the filament tip and the top electrode.

- **Current.** It tunnels across the gap: I = i₀·e^(−g/g₀)·sinh(V/v₀).
- **Gap motion.** The gap moves by thermally activated, field-driven ion drift,
  dg/dt = −ν₀·e^(−Eₐ/kT)·sinh(γa₀V/(t_ox·kT)).
- **Temperature.** T is the filament's own: ambient plus the rise its Joule heat V·I drives
  through a 1 MK/W thermal resistance (an internal thermal node).
- **Feedback.** A smaller gap passes more current, which heats the filament, which speeds the drift.

**Three model choices.**

- **`analysis("static")` sets the initial gap.** At zero bias the drift vanishes *for every gap*,
  so the DC operating point has no unique gap and the matrix row is singular. The model says
  instead: in a static analysis, the gap equals `g_init`; otherwise it obeys the drift equation.
  This is the general pattern for a state that needs a chosen initial value.
- **`$bound_step(0.02·(gmax − gmin)/|drift|)`.** A fast-moving gap asks for steps short enough to
  move it by at most 2 % of its range. The model tells the step controller its own time scale
  instead of the deck having to know it.
- **`gam=8`, the field-enhancement factor.** At twice the value the end of RESET took less than a
  picosecond, and no time step could follow it. The value used keeps the physics and keeps the
  time scales resolvable.

## SET, RESET and temperature (triangular sweep, two ambients)

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/reram_sweep.net --model models/multiphysics/reram --tran --report X1.g,X2.g --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/reram_gap.svg
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/reram_sweep.net --model models/multiphysics/reram --tran --report X1.th,X2.th --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/reram_temp.svg
python docs/examples/multiphysics/reram_iv.py "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

![I–V loops at 300 K and 400 K](examples/multiphysics/reram_iv.svg)
![The filament gap](examples/multiphysics/reram_gap.svg)
![The filament temperature](examples/multiphysics/reram_temp.svg)

**The deck.** Two cells behind 2 kΩ series resistors, the current compliance. One is at
`tamb=300` and one at `tamb=400`. Both are driven by the same triangle,
`PWL(0 0 2.5m 1.6 5m 0 7.5m -1.6 10m 0)`.

**Reporting internal nodes.** `X1.g` is the gap node *inside* instance `X1`, reported as
`Gap(X1.g)` in nanometres. `X1.th` is its thermal node: the filament's temperature rise, in K
above ambient. Neither is a net of the deck, and both are reachable by hierarchical name.

**Why a script for the I–V figure.** The cell current is not an unknown of the circuit; it is
the series resistor's current, (V(in) − V(te))/2 kΩ. `reram_iv.py` reports `in,te1,te2`,
computes it, and plots |I| on a log axis against the cell voltage, the usual way to show a
switching curve.

**The `.tran 1u 10m` card**, and why it is converged. The fast part, RESET, takes about 10 µs
and is resolved by `$bound_step` and the step controller, not by the cap. The run takes 10,181
points in under a second. With a 0.2 µs cap the SET and RESET voltages agree with these to
0.1 mV.

**Event time tolerances.** Both events carry a third argument: `@(above(expr, 1e-9))` and
`@(cross(expr, +1, 1e-9))`. That is a 1 ns time tolerance. A step that reveals a crossing is
re-taken until it lands within 1 ns of it, so the voltage and temperature the strobe prints are
those *at* the crossing. Without it, they belonged to whichever accepted point first fell past
the mid-gap. During a RESET the cell voltage moves tens of mV per step, so the printed voltage
moved with the step size: −0.830 V at a 1 µs cap and −0.852 V at 0.2 µs.

**What the strobes say.**

```text
X2: SET   at t=1.111878e-03 s: V=0.5073 V, I=1.021e-04 A, gap=0.900 nm, T=451.8 K
X1: SET   at t=1.553725e-03 s: V=0.6413 V, I=1.766e-04 A, gap=0.900 nm, T=413.2 K
X2: RESET at t=6.775593e-03 s: V=-0.6960 V, I=-2.202e-04 A, gap=0.900 nm, T=553.3 K
X1: RESET at t=7.527534e-03 s: V=-0.8297 V, I=-3.763e-04 A, gap=0.900 nm, T=612.3 K
```

- **SET is self-limiting.** As the cell conducts, the series resistor takes a growing share of
  the voltage, so the gap closes over 0.58 ms of the ramp.
- **RESET is abrupt and thermal.** It waits until the filament reaches about 610 K, then the
  opening cell takes the voltage back from the resistor, and the gap reopens in 10.5 µs.
- **Arrhenius.** The 400 K cell switches earlier, because e^(−Eₐ/kT) is 1,412 times larger at
  its starting temperature.
- **The loop is pinched.** I = 0 whenever V = 0, whatever the state.

The SET is reported by `@(above(...))`, which also fires at initialization if the condition
already holds. RESET is reported by `@(cross(..., +1))`, the gap passing mid-range while
opening.

## The frequency fingerprint (three decks, one script)

```bash
python docs/examples/multiphysics/reram_loops.py "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

![The pinched loop at 5 kHz, 500 kHz and 5 MHz](examples/multiphysics/reram_loops.svg)

The script runs three decks (`reram_freq_5k.net`, `reram_freq_500k.net`, `reram_freq_5meg.net`),
each a ±1.6 V sinusoid for two periods. It keeps the second period of each and plots the cell
current against the cell voltage.

**Why three decks, and why their time steps differ.** Each deck's `tstep` is a fixed fraction of
its own period:

| Deck | Drive | Card | Cap per period |
|---|---|---|---|
| `reram_freq_5k` | `SIN(0 1.6 5k)` | `.tran 10n 0.4m` | 1/20,000 |
| `reram_freq_500k` | `SIN(0 1.6 500k)` | `.tran 0.1n 4u` | 1/20,000 |
| `reram_freq_5meg` | `SIN(0 1.6 5meg)` | `.tran 10p 0.4u` | 1/20,000 |

A single deck with all three cells would have to run for the slowest drive's two periods
(0.4 ms) at the fastest drive's cap (10 ps): 4·10⁷ steps. That attempt ran for more than
20 minutes. Splitting the decks lets each run at its own time scale.

**What it measures.** A memristor's pinched loop shrinks as the drive outruns its state. The
script integrates the two lobes separately: they are traversed in opposite directions, and a
single signed ∮I dV would cancel them.

| Drive | Gap range over a cycle | Lobe areas (V·A) |
|---|---|---|
| 5 kHz | 0.238–1.697 nm | 3.19·10⁻⁴ + 3.20·10⁻⁴ |
| 500 kHz | 0.759–1.687 nm | 2.19·10⁻⁴ + 2.18·10⁻⁴ |
| 5 MHz | 1.326–1.688 nm | 5.8·10⁻⁵ + 5.8·10⁻⁵ |

# Hodgkin–Huxley axon: propagation, temperature, sodium accumulation {#axon}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/axon/`: `hh_cable.va` and `axon_natures.vams`, which defines a
`gate` discipline (a channel's open probability) and a `chemical` discipline (an intracellular
concentration).

**One module, `N` compartments.** The cable is built inside the model by `generate` loops over a
`genvar`, on vector nets of three disciplines:

```verilog
electrical [0:N-1] v;
gate       [0:N-1] m, h, n;
chemical   [0:N-1] dnai, dki;    // concentration departures from nai0, ki0 (mM)
```

Each compartment carries:

- the 1952 Hodgkin–Huxley Na, K and leak channels;
- its own gates m, h, n;
- its own Na⁺ and K⁺, whose Nernst potentials set ENa and EK.

The concentrations move with the currents, diffuse along the fibre, and relax back through a
first-order pump (`tau_pump`). A second loop links neighbours: axial current, plus longitudinal
ion diffusion.

**Why the concentrations are stored as departures (`dnai`, `dki`).** Newton's first iterate reads
every unknown as zero. A node holding the concentration itself would give ln(Na_o/0) at that
first iterate: an infinite Nernst potential and a NaN residual. As a departure from the initial
value, zero *is* the physical start.

## Conduction velocity, and what temperature does to it

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/hh_giant_axon.net --model models/multiphysics/axon --tran --report X1.v[0],X1.v[50],X1.v[100],X2.v[100] --plot docs/examples/multiphysics/hh_giant_axon.svg
```

![Action potentials along the giant axon](examples/multiphysics/hh_giant_axon.svg)

**The deck.**

```text
VP p gnd PULSE(0 20 0.5m 10u 10u 0.2m 1)
G1 gnd stim1 p gnd 1e-6
G2 gnd stim2 p gnd 1e-6
X1 stim1 hh_cable N=150 len=0.03 a=238e-6 ri=0.354 tc=18.5 probe_a=50 probe_b=100
X2 stim2 hh_cable N=150 len=0.03 a=238e-6 ri=0.354 tc=6.3 probe_a=50 probe_b=100
.tran 10u 6m
```

- **The stimulus** is a current, not a voltage: a 20 V pulse turned into 20 µA by a
  voltage-controlled current source (`G`, gain 1 µS). Each axon gets its own source, so the two
  share a pulse without loading each other.
- **The axon** is `len=0.03 a=238e-6 ri=0.354`: Hodgkin and Huxley's squid axon, 3 cm long,
  radius 238 µm, axoplasm 35.4 Ω·cm, in `N=150` compartments of 0.2 mm.
- **Temperature.** `tc` sets it in °C, and the gating rates scale by Q₁₀ = 3 per 10 °C. Their
  1952 velocity, 18.8 m/s, was computed at **18.5 °C**, so that is the temperature to compare at.
- **The velocity probes.** `probe_a=50 probe_b=100` choose the two compartments, 1 cm apart,
  whose upstrokes through 0 V are timed by `@(cross(V(v[probe_a]), +1))`. The model prints the
  velocity with `$strobe`.

**Reporting inside a vector net.** `X1.v[50]` is element 50 of the vector net `v` inside `X1`.
The plot shows the spike passing compartments 0, 50 and 100 of the warm axon, and compartment
100 of the cold one, late.

**What it prints.**

```text
X1: spike reached compartment 100 at t=1.6572e-03 s; velocity 18.971 m/s
X2: spike reached compartment 100 at t=2.3072e-03 s; velocity 12.218 m/s
```

**18.97 m/s against Hodgkin and Huxley's 18.8 m/s**, 0.9 % above. The cold axon conducts at
12.22 m/s. Its gating runs 3.73× slower, but the velocity falls by only 1.55×, because only the
channels that regenerate the spike slow down, not the cable's passive spread.

### Checking convergence: the time step

`.tran 10u 6m` caps the step at 10 µs. To check that the answer does not depend on it, copy the
deck, change the card to `.tran 2u 6m`, and run it again. The warm axon gives 19.01 m/s, 0.2 %
away, so the 10 µs result is converged to that level.

The cold axon is more sensitive. On its own in a deck it gives 12.35 m/s at a 10 µs cap and
12.29 m/s at 2 µs. In this deck it shares the time steps the warm axon forces, and gives
12.22 m/s. Its figure is good to about 1 %.

### Checking convergence: the number of compartments

Space is checked the same way, by doubling `N` and keeping the probes 1 cm apart:

```bash
sed 's/N=150/N=300/; s/probe_a=50 probe_b=100/probe_a=100 probe_b=200/' circuits/multiphysics/hh_giant_axon.net > /tmp/hh300.net
va-cli sim /tmp/hh300.net --model models/multiphysics/axon --tran --report X1.v[0]
```

With 300 compartments (1803 unknowns, sparse solve) the warm axon gives **18.98 m/s**, against
18.97 m/s with 150 compartments.

::: {.callout-important}
## Parameters that change the model's *structure*

`N` sizes vector nets and bounds `generate` loops, and `probe_a`/`probe_b` index into them. These
values are fixed when the module is **elaborated**, not when it is evaluated. Since 2.15.0, a
device line that sets one of them makes the simulator elaborate the module again for that
value, and it says so on stderr:

```text
[va-cli] elaborated `hh_cable` again for N=300, probe_a=100, probe_b=200: fixed at elaboration (first placed by `X1`)
```

Before 2.15.0 the override reached `dx = len/N` in the analog block, but not the vector
declarations. `N=300` built 150 compartments, each 1/300 of the length, and reported 37.6 m/s.
This tutorial's own convergence check is what found that bug. The same mechanism covers a
parameter whose *default* is computed from another (`parameter real b = 2*a`): it was silently
wrong in the same way, and gave every PMOS in three benchmark decks the NMOS defaults.
:::

## A thin fibre under a spike train: sodium accumulates, ENa falls, spikes shrink

```bash
python docs/examples/multiphysics/hh_thin_fibre.py "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

![Spike peaks follow the falling sodium reversal potential](examples/multiphysics/hh_thin_fibre.svg)

**The deck** (`hh_thin_fibre.net`).

```text
VP p gnd PULSE(0 1 1m 10u 10u 0.5m 10m)
G1 gnd stim p gnd 2e-9
X1 stim hh_cable N=10 len=1e-3 a=0.25e-6 tc=18.5 tau_pump=10 probe_a=2 probe_b=8
.tran 20u 1
```

- **A different fibre from the same model.** Every parameter that differs from the giant axon is
  on the device line: 0.25 µm radius, 1 mm long, 10 compartments, and new probe positions.
  `N=10` and the probes are structural, so this deck too elaborates the module again.
- **The stimulus** is a 2 nA, 0.5 ms pulse every 10 ms, a 100 Hz train for one second
  (`PULSE(... 10m)` repeats with that period).
- **`tau_pump=10`.** A slow pump means the train mostly *accumulates* sodium during the second.
  With the default 1 s, the pump would carry a visible fraction back out.

**Why sodium accumulates here and not in the giant axon.** A spike admits about the same sodium
per unit membrane in both fibres. Behind each square micrometre of membrane, though, there is a/2
of axoplasm. At 0.25 µm instead of 238 µm, the concentration change per spike is about 950× larger.

**A pinned operating point.** With a slow pump in so small a volume, the ion terms outweigh the
pump a thousandfold. Newton's first DC steps carried a concentration through zero, and its
logarithm to NaN. The model therefore pins the concentrations at the DC point with
`analysis("static")`, which is also physically right: the resting state is the initial
concentrations, by definition. This is the same pattern as the ReRAM gap.

**What the script does.** It reports `X1.v[5]` and `X1.dnai[5]` for the middle compartment, and
computes ENa = (RT/F) ln(Na_o/Na_i) from the reported sodium (the model does not output ENa).
It finds each spike's peak and parses the velocity strobes.

| | First spike | 100th spike |
|---|---|---|
| [Na⁺]ᵢ | 55.3 mM | 86.6 mM |
| ENa (Nernst, 18.5 °C) | 52.1 mV | 40.9 mV |
| Spike peak | 29.6 mV | 18.8 mV |
| Conduction velocity | 0.577 m/s | 0.531 m/s |

The peak falls by 10.8 mV as ENa falls by 11.3 mV. Two cross-checks hold:

- The first velocity is the giant axon's scaled by cable theory's √radius law,
  18.97·√(0.25/238) = 0.61 m/s, 5 % away with only 0.1 mm compartments.
- The potassium lost (30.3 mM, `X1.dki[5]`) balances the sodium gained (31.6 mM).

# Power-grid swing: equal areas, relays and a cascade {#grid}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/powergrid/`, which contains:

- `grid_parts.va`: `machine`, `line`, `slack`;
- `grid_natures.vams`: the `grid` discipline (angle in rad as potential, power in pu as flow) and
  `grid_speed` (rotor speed deviation in rad/s).

**The network as a circuit.**

- **A bus.** Its node potential is the voltage phase angle δ.
- **A line.** `Pw(a, b) <+ g·bmax·sin(Ang(a, b))`, a nonlinear conductance between two angle nodes.
- **A machine.** It stamps the swing equation M ω̇ + D ω = Pm − Pe on its bus, with the speed ω on
  an internal node. M = 2H/ω_s comes from the inertia constant `h` and the frequency `f0`.
- **Power balance.** Kirchhoff's current law at a bus is the bus's power balance.

The **DC operating point is therefore the full nonlinear load flow**, with ω = 0 everywhere, and
the transient is the swing.

**Protection as events** (in `line`):

- `@(timer(t_open))` and `@(timer(t_close))` schedule a fault and its clearing (a negative time
  means never);
- `@(cross(abs(p) - pmax, +1))` is an overload relay. It sets `integer open = 1`, which persists
  between events, and the line opens through `g = 1 - transition(open, 0, tsw)`, a 1 ms breaker;
- `@(cross(sin(Ang(a, b)), 0))`, with `cos(Ang(a, b)) < 0` checked in the body, reports every
  passage of the angle across the line through ±180°: a pole slip.

## The equal-area criterion

```bash
python docs/examples/multiphysics/grid_plots.py "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

That one script draws both figures of this section. This one comes from `grid_equal_area.net`:

![Two machines, cleared before and after the critical time](examples/multiphysics/grid_equal_area.svg)

**The deck.**

```text
XINF inf slack
XG1 g1 machine pm=0.8 h=5
XL1 g1 inf line bmax=1.6 t_open=1.0 t_close=1.255
XG2 g2 machine pm=0.8 h=5
XL2 g2 inf line bmax=1.6 t_open=1.0 t_close=1.270
.tran 1m 3
```

- **Two independent machines in one run**, each on its own line to the same infinite bus. G1's
  fault is cleared after 0.255 s and G2's after 0.270 s. Damping is left at its default `d=0`,
  because the equal-area criterion is a statement about an undamped machine.
- **The `slack`** is an infinite bus: an angle source of 0 rad that supplies or absorbs any power.
  It is also the angle reference, which a network otherwise lacks: only angle *differences*
  matter.
- **`.tran 1m 3`.** The swing frequency is 1.05 Hz, so a 1 ms cap is about 950 steps per swing.
  The switching instants are timer breakpoints, landed on exactly.

**Closed form.** With M = 0.031831 s² and Pm/Pmax = 0.5:

- δ₀ = 30°.
- The equal areas give the critical clearing angle 79.56°.
- While the line is open, δ = δ₀ + Pm·t²/2M.
- Together these give **t_cr = 0.2624 s**.

**What the run shows.**

- **G1**, cleared 2.8 % early, peaks at **130.39°** (equal areas: 130.40°) and swings back.
  Undamped, it then oscillates between that and −36.3° indefinitely.
- **G2**, cleared 2.9 % late, passes 150° (180° − δ₀) with speed to spare. Its line reports pole
  slips from t = 1.763 s:

```text
XL2: angle across the line passed 180 degrees at t=1.7631 s (pole slip)
```

### Finding the simulator's own critical clearing time

The pole-slip strobe makes the critical time searchable. This loop bisects the clearing time on a
single machine:

```bash
lo=0.255; hi=0.270
for k in $(seq 1 12); do
  mid=$(python -c "print(round(($lo+$hi)/2,7))")
  printf "* bisect\nXINF inf slack\nXG1 g1 machine pm=0.8 h=5\nXL1 g1 inf line bmax=1.6 t_open=1.0 t_close=%s\n.tran 1m 2.5\n.end\n" \
    "$(python -c "print(1+$mid)")" > /tmp/bisect.net
  if va-cli sim /tmp/bisect.net --model models/multiphysics/powergrid --tran --report g1 2>&1 | grep -q "pole slip"
  then hi=$mid; else lo=$mid; fi
done
echo "t_cr in [$lo, $hi]"
```

It ends at `t_cr in [0.2624267, 0.2624304]`, against the closed form's 0.262366 s: **+0.02 %**.
The 1 ms breaker transition is the only departure from the textbook case.

## A cascade: one line lost, two tripped, two islands

This figure comes from `grid_cascade.net`, drawn by the same script:

![Tie flows, trips, and the islands' frequencies](examples/multiphysics/grid_cascade.svg)

**The deck.**

- **Two areas of four buses**, each a ring of strong lines (`bmax=10`). Area A's machines
  generate (`pm=0.9`) and area B's consume (`pm=-0.9`). All have `h=5 d=0.1` and no governor.
- **Three ties** of different strength, each behind a 1.6 pu relay:

```text
XT1 a1 b1 line bmax=2.5 pmax=1.6
XT2 a2 b2 line bmax=2.0 pmax=1.6
XT3 a3 b3 line bmax=1.5 pmax=1.6 t_open=1.0
```

- **`eps=1e-6` on every machine.** This grid has no infinite bus, so nothing fixes the absolute
  angle. Every angle could shift by the same constant, and the DC operating point's matrix would
  be singular. A leak of 10⁻⁶ pu/rad to the reference fixes the angle level and moves no flow
  measurably.
- **`.tran 1m 10`.** Ten seconds: long enough for the islands to settle at their new
  frequencies.

**The sequence.**

1. **The load flow** shares the 3.6 pu by tie strength: **1.475 / 1.178 / 0.948 pu**, all within
   1.6 pu.
2. **At t = 1 s** a fault opens T3. The remaining ties cannot carry 3.6 pu within their
   settings, and the relays trip them in turn:

   ```text
   XT3: opened at t=1.0000 s (scheduled)
   XT1: TRIPPED at t=1.1494 s, |P| = 1.601 pu > 1.600 pu
   XT2: TRIPPED at t=1.2374 s, |P| = 1.603 pu > 1.600 pu
   ```

3. **The islands settle.** With no governor, each settles where its damping absorbs the
   imbalance: ω = P/ΣD = 3.6/0.4 = 9 rad/s, **±1.4324 Hz**. The run ends at ±1.4323 Hz.
4. **Pole slips.** The open ties report pole slips as the islands drift past each other, about
   75 reports in the remaining nine seconds.

**Why the script, not `--plot`.** The tie flows are not unknowns. The script computes
bmax·sin(δa − δb) from the reported bus angles, and sets each flow to zero from the moment that
line's strobe reports it open. It also converts the speeds `Om(XA1.w)` from rad/s to Hz.

::: {.callout-note}
## A bug this example found (fixed in 2.16.1)

The first cascade run printed 98 `TRIPPED` lines for the two trips that happened. When the
simulator checked an event's condition after each accepted time point, it evaluated the
expression *without the instance's committed state*. `open` read its initial 0 and
`transition()` had no history, so a relay that had opened its line still saw it closed. It
"tripped" again whenever the flow it no longer carried would have crossed 1.6 pu. The answer
was right only because opening an open line changes nothing. Since 2.16.1 the event poll
passes the committed state (`ModelInstance::events_with_state`).
:::

# Thermo-optic ring bank: self-heating, crosstalk and locking {#ring}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/ringbank/`, which contains:

- `ring_parts.va`: `laser`, `ring`, `heater`, `lock`, `thermal_cap`, `thermal_res`;
- `ring_natures.vams`, with four user disciplines.

| Discipline | Potential | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `optical_power` | `Popt`, mW | a guided wave's power |
| `wavelength` | `Wl`, nm | the laser's wavelength, carried beside its power |
| `cmt_field` | `Fld`, √fJ | one quadrature of a ring's intracavity field |
| `ring_heat` | `Temp`, K above the substrate | a ring's temperature (flow `Pwr`, W) |

**Why not the standard `thermal` discipline.** Its natures are defined in a `disciplines.vams`.
When no such file is on the include path, the simulator still accepts `thermal`, but with no
nature behind it: the node prints as `V(t1)` and gets no tolerance of its own. Declaring
`ring_heat` gives the node a name (`Temp(t1) = … K`) and an `abstol`.

**The ring.** Coupled-mode theory, in a frame rotating at the laser's frequency:

$$\frac{da}{dt} = (i\delta - 1/\tau)\,a + \kappa s,\qquad
P_\text{drop} = \tfrac{2}{\tau_e}|a|^2,\qquad P_\text{abs} = \eta\,\tfrac{2}{\tau_i}|a|^2$$

- **The field.** a is complex, so the model carries its real and imaginary parts as two state
  nodes, `ar` and `ai`, each with its own `ddt`.
- **The detuning.** δ comes from the laser's wavelength and the ring's resonance, which moves
  with the ring's temperature at 0.0686 nm/K.
- **Time scales.** τ = 2Q/ω₀ = 16.3 ps, against a 1 ms thermal time constant.

**One-way ports.** A laser's output is a *signal*, not a conserved flow: whatever reads it should
not load it. The model therefore writes it as a potential, `Popt(out) <+ V(pctl)`, and every
reader only probes it. The laser takes its power and wavelength from two electrical nodes, so
ordinary `PWL`, `PULSE` and `DC` sources can drive them (volts read as mW and nm).

**Stiffness.** Picosecond optics and millisecond thermals in one system is a stiffness ratio of
about 10⁸. An explicit integrator would have to step at the photon lifetime: about 10¹¹ steps
for the 2 s sweep below. The implicit trapezoidal default is A-stable, so the fast optical modes
cannot blow up at a 0.5 ms step. The sweep takes 4,094 steps, and Gear (`--integration gear`)
gives the same answers to every printed digit. Neither deck needs a non-default method.

## Self-heating: the thermal triangle and its bistability

```bash
python docs/examples/multiphysics/ring_plots.py "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

![Through-port transmission swept up and down at 0.1 mW and 20 mW](examples/multiphysics/ring_selfheat.svg)

**The deck** (`ring_selfheat.net`):

- **Two rings.** Two laser–ring–thermal-node chains share one wavelength control,
  `VW wctl gnd PWL(0 1549.7 1 1550.6 2 1549.7)`. `VP1 … DC 0.1` and `VP2 … DC 20` set their
  powers.
- **The ring's thermal node** is `XC1 t1 thermal_cap` (2.5·10⁻⁷ J/K) plus
  `XG1 t1 gnd thermal_res` (4000 K/W) to the substrate: τ = 1 ms.
- **`.tran 0.5m 2`.** The sweep is 1 s each way. That is slow against the 1 ms thermal
  constant, so the ring is nearly in thermal equilibrium at every wavelength, which is what makes
  the fold points meaningful. The 0.5 ms cap is half a thermal time constant.

**Why the sweep speed is a parameter, not a detail.** A bistable system's jump happens where its
branch ends, but only in the quasi-static limit. Near a fold the dynamics slow down, so a finite
sweep rate carries the state past the fold before it jumps. The first version of this deck swept
ten times faster, 100 ms per direction. Its jumps landed 0.014 and 0.033 nm past the folds; the
1 s sweep lands 0.004 and 0.009 nm past.

**What the script prints**, with its closed forms:

```text
tau = 16.31 ps, linewidth 0.1564 nm, drop max 0.8116, through min 0.00982, dlambda/dT 0.06864 nm/K
20 mW: hottest 7.1423 K (shift 0.4903 nm), folds at 1550.2545, 1550.4934 nm
X1: through min 0.00982 at 1550.0024 nm
X2: up-sweep jump at 1550.4976 nm, down-sweep snap at 1550.2456 nm, hottest 7.1416 K
```

- **The 0.1 mW ring** is a Lorentzian at the closed-form depth and width. It sits 0.0024 nm red
  of 1550 nm because even 0.1 mW warms it by 0.036 K.
- **The 20 mW ring** has its resonance dragged 0.49 nm by its own heat, the "thermal triangle".
  It is bistable between the two folds, where the sweep direction decides the state.

The closed form behind the folds is the steady state T = R_th·η·(2/τ_i)·|a|², with |a|²
Lorentzian in the *heated* detuning. Solved for the laser wavelength as a function of T, its
turning points are the folds.

**A bug this check caught, in the model.** The first version set τ = Q/ω₀. With da/dt = −a/τ the
*energy* decays at 2/τ, so Q = ω₀τ/2. The dip depth was right, but the linewidth came out
0.3128 nm, twice the closed form. Comparing a single number, such as the dip depth, would not
have caught it.

## A locked bank against crosstalk and self-heating

The same script draws this figure from `ring_bank.net`:

![Drop power and heater power of four locked rings](examples/multiphysics/ring_bank.svg)

**The deck.**

- **Lasers.** Four, at 1550.0/1550.8/1551.6/1552.4 nm and 1 mW.
- **Rings.** Four, made blue of their channels by fabrication: `lambda0=1549.75`, `1550.50`,
  `1551.30` and `1552.15`.
- **Thermal crosstalk.** `XX12 t1 t2 thermal_res r=16000`, and the same between rings 2–3 and
  3–4: a quarter of each ring's own 4000 K/W conductance leaks to its neighbour.
- **Heaters and locks.** `XH1 u1 t1 heater` turns a power command (V(u1) read as mW) into heat.
  `XK1 in1 dr1 u1 lock kp=5 ki=3e3` closes the loop.
- **Disturbances.** At 30 ms, `VW1`'s `PWL` hops channel 1 by +0.2 nm in 10 µs. At 60 ms,
  `VP3`'s steps channel 3's power from 1 to 4 mW.
- **`.tran 50u 100m`.** The 50 µs cap is a twentieth of the thermal constant, fine enough for
  the loop transients. The run takes 2,152 points in about 4 s.

**The lock, parameter by parameter** (`lock` in `ring_parts.va`).

- `frac=0.4` holds the drop power at 40 % of the ring's own input. The set point is relative, so
  a change of input power is not an error: it moves the target with it, and only the physics
  that changes with power, the self-heating, needs correcting.
- `kp=5 ki=3e3` are the PI gains. The plant's gain at the lock point is about 1.4 mW of drop per
  mW of heater: about 5 mW of drop per nm of detuning, times 0.0686 nm/K, times 4 K/mW. The loop
  crosses over well above the thermal pole. The integrator holds the drop *exactly* at the set
  point in steady state, which is what the closed form relies on.
- **Which side of the resonance.** A heater can only red-shift a ring, so from cold each ring
  approaches its laser from the blue side and locks there. That is also the side where
  self-heating is positive feedback (more light → more heat → closer → more light). The loop
  out-gains it.
- **The leak `(1 − g)·V(xi)`.** Before the loop closes (`ton=1e-3`, through `@(timer)` and a
  0.1 ms `transition`), the integrator row would read 0 = 0, and the DC operating point would be
  singular. The leak holds the integrator at zero until then. This is the same pattern as
  `pid.va` in §3.

**What the strobes and the script say.**

```text
XK1: locked at t=0.004921 s, heater 0.5325 mW
XK4: locked at t=0.004921 s, heater 0.5309 mW
XK2: locked at t=0.006371 s, heater 0.8036 mW
XK3: locked at t=0.006371 s, heater 0.8029 mW
 before 30 ms: heaters 0.5323/0.5322  0.8048/0.8048  0.8041/0.8041  0.5306/0.5306  mW (simulated/closed form)
     30-60 ms: heaters 1.4428/1.4428  0.6227/0.6227  0.8041/0.8041  0.5306/0.5306  mW (simulated/closed form)
  after 60 ms: heaters 1.4428/1.4428  0.6227/0.6227  0.6721/0.6721  0.5306/0.5306  mW (simulated/closed form)
```

**The closed form.** With every ring held at its lock temperature, everything that remains is
linear.

- The lock condition fixes each ring's detuning in *frequency*: the drop Lorentzian at 40 %.
- That gives each ring's resonance, so its temperature, so its absorbed heat.
- The heater powers are then G·T − P_abs, with G the thermal network's conductance matrix.

`ring_plots.py` computes this and prints it beside the simulation. It agrees to 10⁻⁴ mW in all
three phases:

- **The hop.** Ring 1's heater rises by (1/4000 + 1/16000)·2.914 K = 0.9105 mW.
- **The crosstalk.** Ring 2's heater falls by 2.914 K/16000 K/W = 0.1821 mW, exactly cancelling
  the heat leaking across.
- **The containment.** Rings 3 and 4 do not move, because ring 2's lock stops the disturbance.
- **The power step.** Ring 3's heater gives back η·(Q_e/Q_i)·0.4·3 mW = 0.1320 mW of
  self-heating.

::: {.callout-note}
## A bug this example found (fixed in 2.16.1)

At the 30 ms hop the run first stopped with `singular matrix during linear solve`. The solve was
not singular: `--solver sparse`, Gear and backward Euler all completed. The dense solver checks
its answer by its residual, and that test compared the raw residual with `1e-6·(1 + ‖b‖)`. A
field row's entries are about 10¹¹ (1/τ and δ in 1/s), so a correct factorisation leaves about
10⁻⁴ of round-off in it, and near Newton convergence b is tiny. The test now measures each row
against its own largest coefficient, so its verdict no longer depends on the units an equation
is written in. Results that passed before are unchanged bit for bit.
:::

# Li-ion cell: kinetics, diffusion, aging and thermal runaway {#liion}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/liion/`, which contains:

- `li_parts.va`: `electrode`, `electrolyte`, `cell_thermal`, `abuse`, `cc_load`;
- `li_natures.vams`, with three user disciplines:

| Discipline | Potential | Flow | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stoich` | `Th`, stoichiometry 0–1 | `Nli`, mol/s of lithium | the diffusion shells |
| `cell_heat` | `Temp`, K | `Pwr`, W | the cell's temperature |
| `extent` | `Ext` | (the row's residual) | a reaction's remaining fraction, or the SEI thickness in nm |

**Building a cell from parts.** A cell is four device lines and a load:

```text
XN1 gnd en1 th1 electrode kind=0 theta0=0.8          graphite: terminal, electrolyte side, heat
XE1 en1 ep1 th1 electrolyte                          the separator, as a resistance
XP1 p1 ep1 th1 electrode kind=1 cmax=51555 vact=2.96e-6 ds=1e-14 k0=6.67e-11 theta0=0.5
XT1 th1 amb cell_thermal                             40 J/K, 0.03 W/K to the node `amb`
XL1 p1 gnd cc_load iset=2                            1C, cut off at 3.0 V
```

`electrode` is one module for both sides. `kind` selects the open-circuit potential with a
`case`, and the cathode's line overrides the material constants. All three parts share the
thermal node `th1`, so every heat they generate lands in the same 40 J/K. The ambient is an
ordinary voltage source whose volts are kelvin: `VA amb gnd DC 298.15`, or a `PWL` for an oven
that ramps.

**Inside `electrode`.**

- **Diffusion.** `stoich [0:N-1] sh` is a vector of N = 10 shells, written with two `generate`
  loops: one gives each shell its lithium capacity (`ddt`), the other links neighbours with
  Fick's conductance.
- **The interface** is on the outermost shell, `sh[N-1]`.
- **The initial state.** `analysis("static")` pins every shell at `theta0` and the film at
  `dsei0`. Without the pin, a DC operating point of a diffusion ladder is any uniform
  stoichiometry, and the matrix would be singular.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Writing Butler–Volmer so that Newton survives it

The textbook form is a current, I = 2·S·i₀·sinh(Fη/2RT). Newton's first iterate reads every node
as 0 V, so the cathode's overpotential there is η = −4.2 V, and sinh of it at 200 K is about
10⁵⁰. That is a conductance no linear solve survives. The model therefore writes the *inverse*,
as a voltage driven by the interface's own branch current:

```verilog
ibv = I(m, e);
eta = 2.0 * `LI_R * t / `LI_F * asinh(ibv / (2.0 * area * i0));
V(m, e) <+ u + eta;
```

It is the same equation, but asinh is smooth everywhere and cannot overflow. A potential
contribution that reads its own branch current is legal Verilog-A, and here it is the difference
between an operating point and none.
:::

## Discharge at three rates

```bash
python docs/examples/multiphysics/li_plots.py "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

This one script runs all three Li-ion decks and draws all three figures.

![Cell voltage against charge delivered](examples/multiphysics/li_discharge.svg)

**The deck** (`li_discharge.net`): three identical cells, loaded at C/20, 1C and 2C
(`cc_load iset=0.1 / 2 / 4`).

- **The load.** `cc_load` switches on at 10 s through `@(timer)` and a 1 s `transition`. It
  switches off through `@(cross(V(p, n) - vmin, -1))`, and its `$strobe` reports the charge
  delivered.
- **`.tran 10 75000`.** The C/20 cell needs about 20 hours; 1C and 2C finish in one hour and
  half an hour. A 10 s cap resolves the 1,333 s thermal constant and the end-of-discharge knee.

**The closed form.** Discharged infinitely slowly, the voltage is the difference of the two
open-circuit potentials as lithium moves from graphite to LiCoO₂. The script finds where it
reaches 3.0 V: **1.9609 Ah**, with the graphite almost empty.

```text
XL3: cutoff at t=1764.4 s (2.9413 V), 1.9493 Ah delivered at 4.000 A
XL2: cutoff at t=3530.4 s (2.9347 V), 1.9558 Ah delivered at 2.000 A
XL1: cutoff at t=70583.6 s (2.9996 V), 1.9604 Ah delivered at 0.100 A
```

- **C/20** comes within 0.03 % of the thermodynamic limit.
- **1C and 2C** lose a little to overpotential, and warm the cells by 3.9 K and 10.8 K.
- **The reported voltage** is the first accepted point *past* the cutoff, which at 1C and 2C
  lands up to 65 mV low because the voltage is falling steeply. A `cross` time tolerance
  (`cross(expr, -1, 1.0)`) would bracket it more tightly.

## Calendar aging: two years on the shelf

![SEI growth and lithium lost at 25, 45 and 60 °C](examples/multiphysics/li_calendar.svg)

**The deck** (`li_calendar.net`): three fully charged cells at open circuit, with ambients of
25, 45 and 60 °C. `sei=1` on the graphite switches on the film.

**The `.tran 1e5 6.3072e7` card.** Two years in steps of up to 10⁵ s, about one per day: 648
steps in about 2 s. Nothing in the cell moves faster than the film, and the film's equation is
smooth, so the cap is a resolution choice for the figure, not an accuracy need.

**The closed form.** The film obeys dδ/dt = k(T)/δ, so δ = √(δ₀² + 2k(T)·t): the parabolic law of
calendar aging. The lithium it consumes is β·S·(δ − δ₀).

```text
calendar 25 C: film 87.1424 nm (closed form 87.1415), lithium lost 0.2105 Ah (closed form 0.2105), OCV 4.1386 V
calendar 45 C: film 164.0769 nm (closed form 164.0743), lithium lost 0.4077 Ah (closed form 0.4077), OCV 4.1281 V
calendar 60 C: film 251.0363 nm (closed form 251.0315), lithium lost 0.6305 Ah (closed form 0.6305), OCV 4.1180 V
```

The script reads the lithium lost from the graphite's stoichiometry: at rest the shells
equalise, so `XN1.sh[0]` is the electrode's average. The tutorial's parameter `ksei=6e-5` is
a calibration choice: at the model's first value, twice this, the 25 °C cell lost 15 % in two
years, more than typical calendar fade.

## Thermal abuse: the oven test

![Cell temperature in three ovens](examples/multiphysics/li_oven.svg)

**The deck** (`li_oven.net`): three cells, each in its own oven, ramped from 25 °C to 130, 135
or 140 °C in 60 s (`PWL(0 298.15 60 403.15)`) and held for ten hours. Each cell is only a
`cell_thermal` and an `abuse` module: no electrochemistry is needed for an oven test.

**The `abuse` module.** Three Arrhenius reactions on `extent` state nodes, with Hatchard et
al.'s rate constants and heats and an 18650's masses:

- SEI decomposition;
- anode–solvent reaction, slowed by the layer it builds;
- cathode–electrolyte reaction, autocatalytic in α(1 − α).

Each `extent` node is pinned to its initial value at DC by `analysis("static")`, and each
reaction's heat goes into the thermal node. `@(cross(Temp(th) - 473.15, +1))` reports the cell
passing 200 °C and what is left of each reactant.

**Finding the threshold.** The same bisection pattern as the power grid's critical clearing
time, on a one-cell deck:

```bash
lo=403.15; hi=408.15
for k in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do
  mid=$(python -c "print(round(($lo+$hi)/2,4))")
  printf "* o\nVO1 o1 gnd PWL(0 298.15 60 $mid)\nXT1 th1 o1 cell_thermal\nXA1 th1 abuse\n.tran 10 36000\n.end\n" > /tmp/oven.net
  if va-cli sim /tmp/oven.net --model models/multiphysics/liion --tran --report th1 2>&1 | grep -q passed
  then hi=$mid; else lo=$mid; fi
done
echo "threshold in [$lo, $hi] K"
```

It ends at `[407.2125, 407.232]`: **134.07 °C** for these parameters. That is the model's
threshold, not a measured cell's.

**What the run shows.**

- **130 °C.** The cell self-heats by 7 K and settles back.
- **135 °C.** It smoulders for four and a half hours, then runs away to 524.5 K. By then the
  slow burn has consumed 83 % of the cathode reactant, which caps the peak.
- **140 °C.** It runs away at t = 5,846 s, to 685.7 K.

**The hard convergence case.** Hours at the 10 s cap, then hundreds of kelvin in seconds, then
back. The step controller covers four decades on its own. The runaway time is step-converged:
5846.2 s at a 10 s cap and 5846.0 s at 2 s.

::: {.callout-note}
## A simulator fix this example needed (2.16.1)

Newton limits each step of a "junction" node to protect `exp(V/V_T)` from overflowing. A module
that declares no junctions gets a guess, and the guess used to be: any `exp` in the module makes
*every* node a junction. In `electrode` the Arrhenius factor alone triggered it, so the cell's
temperature was limited to 0.24 K per Newton step. Starting from 0 K it would have needed about
1,200 iterations, and the operating point failed. Since 2.16.1 the guess applies to electrical
nodes only: a pn junction's voltage limiter says nothing about a temperature.
:::

# Electromagnetic relay: hysteresis, heating, bounce and remanence {#relay}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/relay/`, which contains:

- `relay_parts.va`: `relay_coil`, `armature`, `coil_thermal`;
- `relay_natures.vams`, with four disciplines: `magfield` (A/m), `mech` (m, force as flow),
  `mech_v` (m/s) and `coil_heat` (K, W).

**One coil, three domains.** `relay_coil(p, n, x, th)` couples them all:

- **Electrical port.** `p n`, written as a voltage reading its own current:
  `V(p, n) <+ r * i + nturns * area * MU0 * ddt(Hf(h) + Hf(mm))`.
- **Magnetic circuit.** The internal nodes `h` (field H) and `mm` (magnetization M), with
  Ampère's law as the row of `h`.
- **Mechanical port.** `x`: the gap shrinks as the armature travels, and the magnetic force
  Φ²/(2μ₀A) is applied there.
- **Thermal port.** `th`: R(T) rises 0.393 %/K, and the coil's I²R goes in.

**Jiles–Atherton in an implicit simulator.** The model is an ODE in H whose right-hand side
switches on the sign of dH/dt. Three choices make it solvable:

1. **No differentiated node.** sign(dH/dt) comes from a first-order lag, H − H_lag ≈ τ·dH/dt,
   not from a node holding ddt(H). H is an algebraic unknown, and the trapezoidal rule's
   derivative of an algebraic quantity carries an alternating error that never decays.
2. **Smooth switches.** Both the sign and the irreversible term's on/off gate are tanh-smoothed,
   so dM/dt is continuous at every reversal. With a hard sign, the step controller shrank its
   step to an underflow at the first peak of the drive.
3. **A smoothing scale far below the physics.** `hs` (10 A/(m·s)) must sit well below every real
   dH/dt, or the smoothed sign is less than 1 and the loop depends on the drive's speed. At
   10³ A/(m·s) a 1 s ramp's pickup current moved 0.9 % with the coil's resistance; at 10 it
   moves 0.03 %.

## The B–H loop, and an energy check

```bash
python docs/examples/multiphysics/relay_plots.py "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

![Major and minor B-H loops](examples/multiphysics/relay_bh.svg)

**The deck** (`relay_bh.net`).

- **No gap and no armature.** `relay_coil g0=0` with its `x` port tied to `gnd` makes a closed
  toroid.
- **A current drive.** A sinusoidal *current* comes from a VCCS controlled by a `SIN` voltage:
  `VC1 c1 gnd SIN(0 0.3 50)` and `G1 gnd p1 c1 gnd 1`. H = N·i/l_c then follows the current
  directly, which is how a B–H loop is measured on a bench.
- **`.tran 20u 60m`.** Three periods at 50 Hz, a thousand steps per period. The script uses the
  second period, after the initial magnetization curve.

**The energy check.** Faraday and Ampère make (V − R·I)·I = A·l_c·H·dB/dt exactly, so over one
period the electrical energy the coil keeps equals the loop's area times the core's volume. The
script integrates both sides:

```text
major loop (0.3 A): B max 1.8718 T, remanence 0.570 T, coercivity 380, -385 A/m; loop 3.02190 mJ vs electrical 3.02182 mJ per cycle
minor loop (0.02 A): B max 0.5004 T, remanence 0.362 T, coercivity 375, -374 A/m; loop 0.67668 mJ vs electrical 0.67669 mJ per cycle
```

This is an identity of the equations, so what it checks is the integration: two different
integrals of one run agree to 3·10⁻⁵.

## Pickup, hot pickup, bounce, release and remanence

![Coil voltage and three armatures](examples/multiphysics/relay_switch.svg)

**The deck** (`relay_switch.net`). One coil voltage, `PWL(0 0 1 30 1.5 30 2.5 0 3 0)`, drives
three relays:

- **X1:** coil at 20 °C (`XT1 th1 a20 coil_thermal` against `VA20 a20 gnd DC 293.15`),
  armature travel `xmax=0.8e-3`, so 0.2 mm of air remains when closed.
- **X2:** the same with its coil's ambient at 85 °C, `VA85 a85 gnd DC 358.15`.
- **X3:** coil at 20 °C, `xmax=0.98e-3`, leaving a 20 µm residual gap.

**`.tran 100u 3`.** The 1 s ramps are slow next to the coil's L/R (~0.5 ms) and the armature's
~3 ms travel, so pickup and release are quasi-static. The 100 µs cap and the step controller
resolve the travel and the bounce, which is microseconds.

**What the models print.**

```text
X1: armature lifts at t=0.48856 s: B=0.15882 T, i=0.07320 A, coil 14.6567 V, R 200.027 Ohm
X3: armature lifts at t=0.48856 s: B=0.15882 T, i=0.07320 A, coil 14.6567 V, R 200.027 Ohm
XA1: closed at t=0.50444 s, coil 15.133 V
XA3: closed at t=0.50484 s, coil 15.145 V
X2: armature lifts at t=0.61298 s: B=0.15877 T, i=0.07318 A, coil 18.3894 V, R 251.133 Ohm
XA2: closed at t=0.62942 s, coil 18.883 V
XA2: opened at t=2.41816 s, coil 2.455 V (the closing bounced 1 times)
XA1: opened at t=2.43719 s, coil 1.884 V (the closing bounced 1 times)
```

- **Lift-off.** Force balance at the backstop gives B = √(2μ₀F_pre/A) = 0.15853 T, independent
  of the core. The coils report 0.1588 T; the 0.2 % is the armature already moving.
- **Hot pickup.** The current at lift-off is the same hot or cold (73.2 mA). The voltage scales
  with the coil's resistance: 18.389/14.657 = 1.2547, against R(85 °C)/R(20 °C) = 1.2555, less
  the coil's L·di/dt.
- **Release** is far below pickup, at 1.88 and 2.46 V: when closed, the gap is small and the
  same current makes far more flux.
- **X3 never opens.** With 20 µm of air in the closed magnetic circuit, the core's remanence
  alone holds a flux above the release threshold at zero current. That is the reason for the
  non-magnetic shim on real pole faces, and the residual gap X1 and X2 have.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A model bug that looked like a numerical one

The first version oscillated on its backstop under the default trapezoidal rule and sat still
under backward Euler and Gear. That pattern suggests a stiff mode trapezoidal fails to damp. The
cause was a sign: the backstop's contact damping was −b·v, which pumps energy in. Backward
Euler's own numerical damping outweighed it, and that hid the bug. With the sign fixed, all
three methods agree on every event, and the deck runs with the default.

**The lesson:** when only the dissipative integrators are stable, check the model's energy
balance before blaming the integrator.
:::

# Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion: a pattern-forming grid {#grayscott}

**Library:** `models/multiphysics/grayscott/`: `gray_scott.va` and `rd_natures.vams`, which
defines `reactant` (potential `Cn`, a concentration; flow `Rate`).

**A PDE as a circuit.** The grid is a single module instance:

```verilog
reactant [0:N-1][0:N-1] u, v;           // two 2-D vector nets: one node per cell per species
...
for (i = 0; i < N; i = i + 1) begin : row
    for (j = 0; j < N; j = j + 1) begin : col
        Rate(u[i][j]) <+ ddt(uu) + uu * vv * vv - f * (1.0 - uu);   // the reaction, per cell
        ...
```

A second pair of loops adds the Laplacian as conductances D/h² between neighbours, plus the rows
and columns that wrap around the torus. Those are kept in separate loops so that no unrolled
index is ever out of range.

- **`N` is structural.** It sizes the vector nets and bounds the loops, so a deck that sets
  `N=32` makes the simulator elaborate the module again (§6).
- **`analysis("static")` writes the initial pattern.** At the operating point every cell is
  pinned to Pearson's state: a seeded square, plus a ±1 % perturbation from a hash of the cell's
  indices, the same on every run and platform. The diffusion links are switched off there too,
  or they would pull the pinned values apart.

**Writing files from a model.** The grid is far too large to print as `--report` columns. The
model writes it itself:

```verilog
@(initial_step) if (snap) fd = $fopen("target/gray_scott.txt", "w");
@(initial_step or timer(tsnap, tsnap) or final_step) begin
    if (snap) begin
        $fdisplay(fd, "# %m t=%.6e", $abstime);
        ... $fwrite(fd, "%.5f ", Cn(u[i][j])); ...
    end
    $strobe("%m: t=%.0f s, mean v %.5f, max v %.5f", $abstime, vsum / (N * N), vmax);
end
@(final_step) if (snap) $fclose(fd);
```

Each piece of the event list has a job:

- **`initial_step`.** A `timer` never fires on the run's first point, so `initial_step` writes
  the t = 0 snapshot.
- **`final_step`.** It catches a run whose end is not a multiple of `tsnap`.
- **One body for all three.** When a timer and `final_step` coincide, the `or` list runs the body
  once, not twice. Event `or` lists were added in 2.16.0 for exactly this model.
- **The file name.** `$fopen` takes a literal, so a deck holds one grid that writes the file.
  `snap=0` switches the file off for decks that hold several instances.

## The well-mixed reactor

```bash
va-cli sim circuits/multiphysics/gray_scott_wellmixed.net --model models/multiphysics/grayscott --tran --report X1.u[0][0],X1.v[0][0],X2.u[0][0],X2.v[0][0]
```

**The deck.** Two 2×2 grids with every cell alike (`seed=2` covers the grid, `amp=0`), so
nothing diffuses and each cell is one stirred reactor. The control parameters are F = k = 0.04,
and the two grids start on opposite sides of the separatrix:

- `X1 ref gray_scott N=2 f=0.04 k=0.04 seed=2 u_seed=0.3 v_seed=0.35 amp=0 snap=0`;
- the same with `u_seed=0.9 v_seed=0.05`.

**The closed form.** Steady states satisfy u·v = F + k and F(1 − u) = u·v²:

- (1, 0), stable;
- (0.8, 0.1), a saddle;
- (0.2, 0.4), a stable focus (Jacobian trace −0.12, determinant 0.0096).

The run ends at `Cn(X1.u[0][0])=0.200000 Cn(X1.v[0][0])=0.400000` and `Cn(X2.u[0][0])=1.000000
Cn(X2.v[0][0])=3.579108e-71`: the two stable states, reached from either side of the saddle.

## Self-replicating spots

```bash
python docs/examples/multiphysics/gray_scott.py gray_scott_spots "$PWD/target/release/va-cli"
```

![Gray-Scott spots on a 32 x 32 torus](examples/multiphysics/gray_scott_spots.svg)

**The deck** (`gray_scott_spots.net`): a single line,
`X1 ref gray_scott N=32 len=0.32 f=0.0367 k=0.0649 seed=3 tsnap=1000`.

- **The grid.** 32×32 cells of 0.01, Pearson's resolution: 2049 unknowns, which selects the
  sparse solver.
- **`.tran 20 6000`.** A 20 s step cap. The first trials used 5 s; 20 s gives the same pattern
  (mean v at t = 5000: 0.09161 against 0.09161; max v 0.36331 against 0.36333) in 97 s instead of
  225 s.
- **Speed.** One instance means the instance-parallel evaluation has nothing to share out, which
  is why a 2049-unknown grid takes a minute and a half.

**What the script prints.** For each snapshot: the mean and maximum of v, and the number of
spots, counted as regions with v > 0.3 on the torus (a spot that crosses the grid's edge is one
region):

```text
t=       0: mean v 0.00850, max v 0.25000, 0 region(s) with v > 0.3
t=    1000: mean v 0.02646, max v 0.34173, 1 region(s) with v > 0.3
t=    2000: mean v 0.03532, max v 0.40045, 2 region(s) with v > 0.3
t=    3000: mean v 0.07948, max v 0.40306, 4 region(s) with v > 0.3
t=    4000: mean v 0.09133, max v 0.36495, 4 region(s) with v > 0.3
t=    5000: mean v 0.09161, max v 0.36331, 4 region(s) with v > 0.3
t=    6000: mean v 0.09166, max v 0.36372, 4 region(s) with v > 0.3
```

**What the run shows.**

- **Mitosis.** One spot divides into two, then four, which tile the torus. In the figure, spots
  straddling the edge appear as halves.
- **Labyrinths need a bigger torus.** The labyrinth parameters (F = 0.029, k = 0.057) on the same
  32×32 grid make a single ring: the domain is too small for the pattern's wavelength. On 48×48
  they grow into nested rings that keep the seed's four-fold symmetry, because the ±1 %
  perturbation is too weak to break it. That run takes about 16 minutes, which is why it is not a
  deck.

# Reproducing every figure

From the repository root, after `cargo build --release`, with `va-cli` aliased as in §2.1.
`VA` is the absolute path the scripts need.

```bash
VA="$PWD/target/release/va-cli"        # Git Bash on Windows: VA="$(pwd -W)/target/release/va-cli.exe"
M=models/multiphysics
C=circuits/multiphysics
F=docs/examples/multiphysics

# Peltier cooler
va-cli sim $C/tec_dtmax.net  --model $M/tec --report cold --plot $F/tec_dtmax.svg
va-cli sim $C/tec_energy.net --model $M/tec
va-cli sim $C/tec_pid.net    --model $M/tec --tran --report plate,sink --plot $F/tec_pid_temps.svg
va-cli sim $C/tec_pid.net    --model $M/tec --tran --report drv        --plot $F/tec_pid_drive.svg

# MEMS
va-cli sim $C/mems_pullin.net     --model $M/mems        --report x       --plot $F/mems_pullin.svg
va-cli sim $C/mems_resonance.net  --model $M/mems --ac   --report xlo,xhi --plot $F/mems_resonance.svg
va-cli sim $C/mems_hysteresis.net --model $M/mems --tran --report x       --plot $F/mems_hysteresis.svg

# ReRAM
va-cli sim $C/reram_sweep.net --model $M/reram --tran --report X1.g,X2.g   --plot $F/reram_gap.svg
va-cli sim $C/reram_sweep.net --model $M/reram --tran --report X1.th,X2.th --plot $F/reram_temp.svg
python $F/reram_iv.py "$VA"
python $F/reram_loops.py "$VA"

# Hodgkin-Huxley axon
va-cli sim $C/hh_giant_axon.net --model $M/axon --tran --report X1.v[0],X1.v[50],X1.v[100],X2.v[100] --plot $F/hh_giant_axon.svg
python $F/hh_thin_fibre.py "$VA"

# Power grid
python $F/grid_plots.py "$VA"

# Thermo-optic ring bank
python $F/ring_plots.py "$VA"

# Li-ion cell
python $F/li_plots.py "$VA"

# Relay
python $F/relay_plots.py "$VA"

# Gray-Scott
va-cli sim $C/gray_scott_wellmixed.net --model $M/grayscott --tran --report X1.u[0][0],X1.v[0][0],X2.u[0][0],X2.v[0][0]
python $F/gray_scott.py gray_scott_spots "$VA"
```

Approximate run times on the development laptop (Intel i7-1185G7):

| Run | Time |
|---|---|
| each TEC and MEMS run, the equal-area deck, each ring deck | under 5 s |
| grid cascade | about 6 s |
| ReRAM triangular sweep | under 1 s |
| ReRAM frequency decks (`reram_loops.py` runs all three) | about 1 min each |
| giant-axon pair | about 1.5 min |
| thin-fibre train | about 2 min |
| the three Li-ion decks (`li_plots.py`) | about 30 s together |
| the two relay decks (`relay_plots.py`) | about 40 s together |
| Gray–Scott spots (2049 unknowns) | about 1.5 min |

These were measured with other simulations running on the same machine, so they are upper
bounds.
